title: Passive with modals and perfect forms
objectives: Form passive clauses with modals and perfect forms.
Distinguish active continuous from passive structures.
Use optional by phrases to identify agents.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Passive forms allow us to focus on the person or thing affected by an action. ‘The technician can repair the device’ and ‘The device can be repaired’ describe the same possible repair, but the passive makes the device the subject. A by phrase can identify the agent when relevant: ‘The device can be repaired by a technician’.

Passive structures can combine with modal verbs and perfect aspect. ‘The report must be submitted today’ expresses an obligation in the passive. ‘The report has been submitted’ presents submission as completed with present relevance. ‘The report must have been submitted already’ can express a strong deduction about a completed past submission.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: For a basic modal passive, use modal plus be plus a past participle: ‘can be repaired’, ‘should be checked’ and ‘must be submitted’. For a present perfect passive, use have or has been plus a past participle: ‘The documents have been signed’. For a past perfect passive, use had been plus a past participle: ‘The documents had been signed before the meeting’.

For a modal perfect passive, use modal plus have been plus a past participle: ‘The letter might have been delivered’ or ‘It must have been sent’. The modal expresses the speaker's judgement or another meaning; the passive structure identifies the affected subject. Negatives and questions depend on the first auxiliary: ‘Has it been checked?’ and ‘It hasn't been checked’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘The technician has repaired the device’ with ‘The device has been repaired by the technician’. The active subject becomes the optional agent in the by phrase, while the object becomes the passive subject. Compare ‘Someone might have sent the letter’ with ‘The letter might have been sent’: both describe possibility about a past event.

Distinguish ‘She has been repairing the device’ from ‘The device has been repaired’. The first is present perfect continuous active and focuses on her activity. The second is present perfect passive and presents the device as affected by a completed repair. Been appears in both, but the following form and the subject's role differ.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not omit be in a basic modal passive: ‘must be checked’, not ‘must checked’. Do not omit been in a present perfect passive: ‘has been signed’, not ‘has signed’ when the document is the affected subject. Use a past participle after been, as in written or sent.

A passive sentence need not name the agent. Choose a by phrase when identifying the agent helps the reader; avoid adding one merely to make a sentence longer. Modal meaning remains important: ‘must be repaired’ may express obligation, whereas ‘must have been repaired’ may express a deduction about an earlier repair in the relevant context.

examples.note: Can be plus a participle forms a modal passive.

examples.sentence: The report must be submitted today.
examples.note: Must expresses obligation in a basic modal passive.
Have been plus a participle forms the present perfect passive.

examples.sentence: The documents had been signed before the meeting.
examples.note: Had been plus a participle forms the past perfect passive.

examples.sentence: The letter might have been sent.
examples.note: Might have been plus a participle expresses a possible past event in the passive.

examples.sentence: The report must have been submitted already.
examples.note: Must can express a strong past deduction in this context.
Has moves before the subject in a question.

examples.sentence: The device has been repaired by a technician.
examples.note: The by phrase identifies the agent.

common_errors.reason: Use be before the participle in the modal passive.
Use the participle sent after been.

common_errors.incorrect: The documents have signed by Ana.
common_errors.correct: The documents have been signed by Ana.
common_errors.reason: Use been in this present perfect passive.

summary: Use modal plus be plus a participle for a basic modal passive.
Use have, has or had been plus a participle for the corresponding perfect passive.
Use modal plus have been plus a participle for a modal perfect passive.

exercises.prompt: The report must ___ today. (submit; passive)
exercises.explanation: Must be submitted is the basic modal passive.

option_feedback.a: “submitted” does not fit here. Must be submitted is the basic modal passive.
option_feedback.b: “been submit” does not fit here. Must be submitted is the basic modal passive.
option_feedback.c: “have submit” does not fit here. Must be submitted is the basic modal passive.
option_feedback.d: “be submitted” fits here. Must be submitted is the basic modal passive.

exercises.prompt: The documents ___ already. (sign; present perfect passive)
exercises.explanation: Have been signed is the present perfect passive with a plural subject.

option_feedback.a: “have been signed” fits here. Have been signed is the present perfect passive with a plural subject.
option_feedback.b: “have signed by Ana” does not fit here. Have been signed is the present perfect passive with a plural subject.
option_feedback.c: “have been sign” does not fit here. Have been signed is the present perfect passive with a plural subject.
option_feedback.d: “has being signed” does not fit here. Have been signed is the present perfect passive with a plural subject.

exercises.prompt: The letter might ___ yesterday. (send; modal perfect passive)
exercises.explanation: Might have been sent is the modal perfect passive.

option_feedback.a: “be sent yesterday already has” does not fit here. Might have been sent is the modal perfect passive.
option_feedback.b: “have being sent” does not fit here. Might have been sent is the modal perfect passive.
option_feedback.c: “have been sent” fits here. Might have been sent is the modal perfect passive.
option_feedback.d: “have been send” does not fit here. Might have been sent is the modal perfect passive.

exercises.prompt: The road ___ before the meeting began. (repair; past perfect passive)

option_feedback.d: “had be repaired” does not fit here. Had been repaired is the past perfect passive.

option_feedback.a: “Does” does not fit here. Has precedes the singular subject in the question.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is present perfect continuous active?
exercises.explanation: Has been repairing describes her activity in the active voice.

options.text: She has been repairing the device.

option_feedback.a: “The device has been repaired.” does not fit here. Has been repairing describes her activity in the active voice.
option_feedback.b: “She has been repairing the device.” fits here. Has been repairing describes her activity in the active voice.
option_feedback.c: “The device might be repaired.” does not fit here. Has been repairing describes her activity in the active voice.
option_feedback.d: “The device was repaired.” does not fit here. Has been repairing describes her activity in the active voice.
